summary: The base TRILL protocol forwards Layer 2 traffic within a subnet optimally, but traffic between subnets usually goes through a centralized gateway, which has drawbacks. This proposed standard describes a distributed layer 3 gateway for TRILL, so inter-subnet traffic can be routed more directly.

eli5.summary: Imagine every mail trip has to go through a single central post office even when you live next door. This lets many local offices do the passing-along work so mail takes shorter trips.

subtitle: Letting every edge switch in a TRILL network route between subnets instead of detouring through a central gateway.

tldr.problem: Base TRILL forwards traffic within a subnet optimally, but traffic between subnets normally goes through a centralized gateway. That gives sub-optimum paths, a gateway that needs a huge number of interfaces, and a possible bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: Each edge RBridge acts as the Layer 3 gateway for its own end stations, with a separate routing instance per tenant. Edge RBridges share tenant labels, gateway MACs and IP prefixes through new IS-IS APPsub-TLVs, and send inter-subnet traffic straight to the egress RBridge in a TRILL packet.
tldr.outcome: Both intra-subnet and inter-subnet unicast traffic can follow optimal pair-wise paths, with inter-subnet traffic spread over all edge RBridges. The scheme is optional.

today: RFC 7956 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The distributed gateway is an optional feature of TRILL.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) gives least-cost transparent routing in multi-hop networks using IS-IS link-state routing and a hop count. TRILL switches are also called RBridges. The base protocol is optimal for Layer 2 traffic inside a subnet but not for Layer 3 traffic between subnets, where a subnet normally has its own IP prefix and its own Data Label (a VLAN or a Fine-Grained Label, FGL).

With the distributed gateway, an edge RBridge routes by Layer 2 identity among end stations (ESs) in the same subnet and by Layer 3 identity among ESs in different subnets of the same routing domain. Each edge RBridge needs routing instances and gateway interfaces for its locally connected ESs. The routing instances keep tenants' IP address spaces isolated. Inter-subnet traffic is spread over the edge RBridges, so there is no single bottleneck.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big mailroom for the whole building, every floor gets its own small mailroom that can send letters straight to another floor.

sections.title: The Problem with a Centralized Gateway
sections.content:
Inside one subnet, an ES just ARPs for the destination's MAC address and TRILL delivers the frame to the right edge RBridge. Between subnets, packets typically go to an L3 gateway that routes and, if needed, changes the Data Label.

In the RFC's data-center example, all traffic between VLANs goes through the centralized gateway on COR1 or COR2, even between two ESs on the same top-of-rack switch, because only the gateway can change the VLAN labeling. The RFC lists three issues:

  1. Sub-optimum forwarding paths for inter-subnet traffic.
  2. A gateway may need a very large number of interfaces, one per tenant per Data Label used by that tenant.
  3. A possible traffic bottleneck at the gateway.

With FGL, in theory up to 16 million L2 virtual networks could be supported in a TRILL campus, which makes the interface count worse.
sections.eli5: If two friends in the same classroom could only pass notes by sending them to the principal's office first, notes would be slow and the office would be swamped.

sections.title: The Distributed Gateway Design
sections.content:
Each tenant normally corresponds to one routing domain, and each L2 virtual network (VN) is identified by a unique 12-bit VLAN ID or 24-bit FGL. Each edge RBridge keeps a VRF (virtual routing and forwarding instance) per tenant, so overlapping IP address space does not clash. A Tenant ID, unique across the campus, names each routing domain. The operator MUST configure Tenant IDs consistently on every edge RBridge, otherwise data might reach the wrong tenant.

The edge RBridge answers ARP/ND requests for the gateway IP with its gateway MAC. When an ES sends traffic to that MAC, the RBridge ends the Ethernet header, looks up the destination in that tenant's routing table and, for a remote ES, re-encapsulates the packet:

  • Inner.MacSA is the ingress RBridge's gateway MAC.
  • Inner.MacDA is the egress RBridge's gateway MAC.
  • The inner Data Label identifies the tenant.
  • The outer TRILL header uses the egress RBridge's nickname.

All edge RBridges are several TRILL hops apart but only one IP hop away. If equal-cost shortest paths exist, all can be used, which spreads the load. Gateway MAC and gateway IP configuration SHOULD be shared by edge RBridges that serve the same subnet, which can be done by local configuration and NETCONF/YANG models.
sections.eli5: Each local mailroom wears the same badge for its floor. When a letter goes to another floor, the mailroom re-labels it for the destination mailroom and sends it down the shortest hallway.

sections.title: Learning and Sharing Routes
sections.content:
An edge RBridge learns local IP and MAC pairs through ARP/ND and creates local IP routes. A router behind the edge RBridge looks like an ES to TRILL. That router SHOULD run an IP routing protocol with the edge RBridge. Without one, only prefixes explicitly configured on the RBridge are reachable.

When a routing instance is created, its Tenant ID, tenant Data Label and tenant gateway MAC are configured and MUST be globally advertised. Edge RBridges also advertise local IP prefixes with the Tenant ID. If a VN's ESs are on several RBridges, each MUST advertise every local ES address. If they are on only one, it can advertise the subnet as a host route. The information travels in E-L1FS FS-LSP APPsub-TLVs, and each RBridge builds remote routing entries from it.

Timing rules protect traffic in flight:

  • A deleted tenant may cause brief inconsistency. In-flight traffic is dropped at the egress RBridge.
  • A tenant Data Label MUST NOT be reallocated until a reasonable time has passed, for example twice the IS-IS Holding Time.
  • If an ARP entry times out, the RBridge advertises the deletion of that route.
  • If a gateway MAC changes, in-flight traffic using the old MAC is discarded or forwarded as L2 intra-subnet traffic.

An RBridge with several nicknames can mark one as the inter-subnet egress nickname. If an ES is attached to two RBridges in active-active mode, both MUST be configured as distributed gateways. The ingress RBridge then sees two IP next hops and picks by least cost or local load balancing.
sections.eli5: Each mailroom writes down who lives on its floor and tells all the other mailrooms. If someone moves out, it sends a correction, and any letters still on the way are thrown away.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example has RB1 and RB2 as distributed gateways. ES1 is in VLAN 10 on RB1 and ES2 is in VLAN 20 on RB2, both in Tenant1. Both RBridges use tenant label VLAN 100 and have their own gateway MAC (MAC1 and MAC2). RB3 and RB4 are transit RBridges.

Each RBridge advertises its tenant ID, gateway MAC, tenant label and prefixes. RB1 then holds a remote route for ES2's subnet pointing at MAC2, inner VLAN 100 and egress nickname nick2.

When ES1 sends to ES2, RB1 sees its own gateway MAC as the destination, ends the L2 header, finds the route and encapsulates with MAC2 as Inner.MacDA, MAC1 as Inner.MacSA, VLAN 100 as Inner.VLAN, nick2 as egress and nick1 as ingress. A transit RBridge forwards by nickname. RB2 decapsulates, sees its own gateway MAC, uses the inner VLAN to find the VRF, and delivers to ES2 in VLAN 20.
sections.eli5: A letter from room A goes to its floor's mailroom, gets a new label for the other floor's mailroom, and rides the hallway. The far mailroom opens it and hands it to the right door.

sections.title: TRILL Protocol Extensions
sections.content:
Participating RBridges announce their information with new IS-IS APPsub-TLVs, which MUST be included in a TRILL GENINFO TLV in E-L1FS FS-LSPs.

  • Tenant Label and Gateway MAC (type 7, TENANT-GWMAC-LABEL): a 4-byte Tenant ID, a 12-bit label for a VLAN (Length 12) or a two-part 24-bit label for an FGL (Length 14), and the 6-byte tenant gateway MAC. Reserved bits MUST be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.
  • SE flag in the NickFlags APPsub-TLV: if set to 1, the advertising RBridge suggests that nickname SHOULD be used as the inter-subnet egress nickname. The flag is ignored if the sender does not own the nickname.
  • IPv4 Prefix (type 8, IPV4-PREFIX) and IPv6 Prefix (type 9, IPV6-PREFIX): a 4-byte Tenant ID followed by one or more prefix-length and prefix pairs. A prefix length of 0 matches all addresses of that family.

IANA assigned types 7, 8 and 9 in the TRILL APPsub-TLV registry and bit 1 (SE) in the NickFlags Bits registry.
sections.eli5: These are the standard forms the mailrooms use to tell each other who lives where: which tenant, which badge, which addresses.

sections.title: Security and Management
sections.content:
Correct configuration of the edge RBridges matters, because wrong configuration could deliver data to the wrong tenant. IS-IS security (RFC 5310) can protect the advertisements. The label reuse and gateway MAC rules above avoid mishandling traffic in flight. Choosing tenant labels and IDs pseudorandomly (RFC 4086) makes them harder for an adversary to guess. Sensitive data should be encrypted end to end between ESs.

For management, the distributed gateway configuration at each RBridge is visible to all other RBridges through the link-state database. TRILL OAM is covered in RFC 7455 and RFC 7456.
sections.eli5: If a mailroom has the wrong badge, mail could go to the wrong family, so everyone must set things up carefully. Private letters should be sealed so only the receiver can read them.
